name: Sakshinatheswarar Temple, Tirupurambayam
deity: Shiva as Sakshinatheswarar (Satchinadeswarar, Punnaivananathar), with the goddess Karumpadu Solliammai
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of Chola Nadu, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); present masonry largely of the Nayak period (16th century)
dynasty: Chola associations; present structure of the Nayak period
summary: Sakshinatheswarar, the Lord Who Bore Witness, is the Shiva temple of Tirupurambayam near Kumbakonam, sung by Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar, in a village remembered both for the tale of divine testimony and for a battle that shaped Chola history.

sections.history: Tirupurambayam, a village of the Chola country near Kumbakonam, is sung in the Tevaram by Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar, and counts among the Paadal Petra Sthalams north of the Kaveri. The ground is historic in another sense too: around 880 CE the battle of Thirupurambiyam was fought here, in which the Pallava king Aparajita, joined by a Western Ganga ally and the Chola prince Aditya I, overcame the Pandya king Varaguna II. Accounts differ on the date and details, but the battle is remembered as a turning point on the road to the imperial Cholas, and one tradition says Aditya I raised a temple here in remembrance. The masonry seen today is largely of the Nayak period, the sixteenth century, while the shrine of the goddess is credited to Rajaraja I.
sections.architecture: The temple has two gateway towers, of which the western is the taller, rising five storeys to about 72 feet. Sakshinatheswarar, also called Satchinadeswarar and Punnaivananathar, presides in the sanctum, and the goddess Karumpadu Solliammai has her own shrine. The sacred tree is the punnai, and the temple's holy water is the Brahma theertham. The shrine of Vinayaka draws special devotion: on Vinayagar Chaturthi the image is anointed with honey, and the honey is said to be wholly absorbed by the stone. A vanni tree stands within the precincts, though it is not the sacred tree.
sections.legends: The temple takes its name from a story that the Tiruvilaiyadal Puranam counts among the sacred plays of the Lord of Madurai. A young woman of a merchant family was married here to a kinsman with no human guests, only a vanni tree, a well and the Lord himself as witnesses, and in some tellings the kitchen where the couple stayed. When the man later denied the marriage, the Lord went to Madurai with those witnesses and testified, and he has been Sakshinathar, the Lord who bore witness, ever since. The vanni tree is said to stand still in a corner of the Madurai Sundareswarar temple, though tellings differ in their details. A second legend explains the village's survival: when the great deluge came, Vinayaka drew the waters of the seven seas into a well here and spared the place.
sections.festivals: Vinayagar Chaturthi is the day this temple is best known for, when the shrine of Vinayaka is bathed in honey that the image is said to absorb entirely. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. A fuller festival calendar was not available, so confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Tirupurambayam is a quiet place to reflect on trust and truth. Pass beneath the tall western gopuram, pause at the shrine of Vinayaka, and come to Sakshinatheswarar before visiting the goddess Karumpadu Solliammai. Devotees pray here for honesty in dealings and for promises to be kept, and many ask the Lord to witness vows made in good faith. The village lies amid Kaveri paddy fields a few kilometres from Kumbakonam, and standing there one can recall both the Lord who testified and the old battlefield that gave the place its mark on history.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; timings are not firmly sourced, so confirm locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tirupurambayam is about 10 km from Kumbakonam (listings give between 9 and 11 km), and Kumbakonam, the nearest railway station, is the main base for buses and taxis. The village lies a few kilometres off the Kumbakonam–Swamimalai road. Tiruchirappalli, with the region's airport, is roughly 90 km away.
